::: {.lead}
Today you test AI answers like a checker, and you use AI honestly. Each
experiment has two parts. **Part A** is in an AI assistant, a search engine
and Word on the lab computer. **Part B** is on a simulator of the
interactive lesson: on paper, scan its QR code; on the screen, click its
link. After each step, write your result in its box. At the end, copy your
key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a lab computer with a browser, an AI assistant that the
  university allows (for example `copilot.microsoft.com`), a search engine
  (`bing.com`) and Word.
- **No lab computer today?** Your teacher does Part A on the screen, on the
  simulators of the interactive lesson and in an AI assistant. Do Part B on your phone.
- **Never type personal data** into an AI tool: this lecture shows how to
  keep it out.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

## Experiment 1 · Claims and sources

**The idea:** a **claim** is a sentence that can be checked: a number, a
date, a name, a fact. Check each claim outside the AI, in two **reliable
sources** that agree. An AI can give a **made-up source**: search its
title, check its authors, and open its link; if one check fails, delete
it.

**Aim:** check an AI claim in two sources outside the AI.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the apps (an AI assistant and a search engine)**
:::

1. Copy this prompt into an AI assistant. Then check the answer in **two
   reliable sources**, for example an encyclopedia and a map site.

   ::: {.prompt}
   What is the highest mountain in Jordan, and how high is it?
   :::

   {{< record "The AI says … ; my two sources say …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Two reliable sources give **Jabal Umm al-Dami** (جبل أم الدامي), about
   **1 850 m**, in the south near Wadi Rum. If the AI named another mountain
   or another height, correct it with the sources.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   An AI says: "The highest mountain in Jordan is Jabal Ram, 1 734 m." Two
   reliable sources say Jabal Umm al-Dami, about 1 850 m. What do you write?

   - [x] Jabal Umm al-Dami, about 1 850 m

     Why: Two reliable sources that agree show a true claim: correct the AI with the sources.

   - [ ] Jabal Ram, 1 734 m

     Why: One AI answer is not a source.

   - [ ] Nothing: the AI and the sources disagree.

     Why: Two reliable sources that agree are enough to correct the AI.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/fact-check-lab.html" poster="sims/fact-check-lab.png" title="Fact-Check Lab: Sami's AI draft" >}}

2. In **Fact-Check Lab**, tap each of the six claims of Sami's text, read
   the search results, and decide: keep, correct or remove.

   {{< record "Correct … ; remove …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Keep:** 7 hours of sleep, and a short nap of 20 minutes.
   **Correct:** the brain uses about 20 % (not 50 %), and the library opens
   at 8:00 (not 7:00). **Remove:** Miller & Hart (2019) and the Einstein
   quote: nothing reliable shows them.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Keep, correct or remove? Sort the six claims of Sami's text.

   Keep
   :   We need about 7 hours of sleep.

       Why: Reliable sources agree.

   :   A short nap lasts 20 minutes.

       Why: Reliable sources agree.

   Correct
   :   The brain uses 50 % of the body's energy.

       Why: Sources say about 20 %.

   :   The library opens at 7:00.

       Why: The library page says 8:00.

   Remove
   :   A study by Miller & Hart (2019)

       Why: Nothing reliable shows this study: a made-up source.

   :   The quote of Einstein

       Why: Nothing reliable shows that he said it.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Bias

**The idea:** **bias** in an AI text is an unfair idea from its data: "the
nurse … she", "a young man", one side only. Check **who** the text shows
and **how**. Ask for neutral language, different people, and both sides
with reasons.

**Aim:** find bias in an AI text, and ask for a fair one.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (an AI assistant)**
:::

1. Copy this prompt. Does the advert say anything about gender, age or
   origin? Then ask, in the same chat: *Rewrite it in neutral language.
   Describe the job, not the person.* Paste the fair advert into Word:
   `job-advert.docx`.

   ::: {.prompt}
   Write a short job advert for a warehouse worker.
   :::

   {{< record "Words about the person (or: none) … ; one fair requirement …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Look for words such as "young", "strong man" or "he": they are about the
   person, not the job. A fair requirement is about the work, for example
   "You lift boxes of up to 20 kg" or "You use a computer for the lists".
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   About the job, or about the person? Sort the lines of a job advert.

   About the job: keep it
   :   You lift boxes of up to 20 kg.

       Why: It describes the work.

   :   You use a computer for the lists.

       Why: A skill that the job needs.

   About the person: bias
   :   We need a young man.

       Why: Age and gender are not the job.

   :   You must be from Amman.

       Why: Origin is not the job.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/bias-lab.html" poster="sims/bias-lab.png" title="Bias Lab: who does the AI show, and how?" >}}

2. In **Bias Lab**, do the three requests. For each one, add the instruction
   that removes the red parts.

   {{< record "Doctor and nurse … ; trainee and accountant … ; working from home …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Doctor and nurse:** use neutral language. **Trainee and accountant:**
   use neutral language and show different people. **Working from home:**
   give both sides with reasons.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   An AI text about working from home gives only its good sides. Which
   instruction makes it fair?

   - [x] Give both sides with reasons.

     Why: A fair text shows the good and the bad sides.

   - [ ] Use neutral language.

     Why: Neutral words do not add the missing side.

   - [ ] Make it shorter.

     Why: A shorter text can still show one side only.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · Safe prompts and an honest statement

**The idea:** never type personal data into an AI tool: names, phone
numbers, addresses, ID numbers or grades of real people. Write a
**placeholder** instead, for example [name] or [phone], and add the real
details later, outside the AI. When you use AI for your work, say so: an
**AI-use statement** names the tool, says what the AI did, what you changed
and how you checked it.

**Aim:** clean a prompt, and say honestly how you used AI.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Word)**
:::

1. Write this prompt again with placeholders, in Word: *Write a short
   message to my neighbour Khaled Nasser, phone 0790000000, of 5 Olive
   Street: the water tank on our roof leaks, and a plumber comes on Tuesday
   at 10:00.*

   {{< record "My clean prompt" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good prompt: "Write a short message to **[neighbour]**, phone
   **[phone]**, of **[address]**: the water tank on our roof leaks, and a
   plumber comes on Tuesday at 10:00." The leak, Tuesday and 10:00 stay:
   the AI needs them.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which prompt is clean?

   - [x] Write a short message to [neighbour], phone [phone], of [address]: the water tank on our roof leaks, and a plumber comes on Tuesday at 10:00.

     Why: The personal data has placeholders; the leak, Tuesday and 10:00 stay.

   - [ ] Write a short message to Khaled Nasser, phone 0790000000, of 5 Olive Street: the water tank on our roof leaks …

     Why: The name, the phone and the address are personal data.

   - [ ] Write a short message to [neighbour]: [problem] on [day] at [time].

     Why: The AI needs the leak, the day and the time; they say nothing about who the person is.
   :::

2. Under the job advert, write an AI-use statement of three or four
   sentences: the tool, what the AI did, what you changed, how you checked
   it. Save the file.

   {{< record "My first sentence … ; the part that was missing (or: none) …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A good statement: "I used Microsoft Copilot to write a first job advert
   for a warehouse worker. I asked it for neutral language and wrote two
   tasks in my own words. I checked that every requirement is about the
   job." The part that students forget most is **the check**.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Which part of the statement is each sentence? Sort them.

   The tool
   :   I used Microsoft Copilot.

       Why: It names the AI tool.

   What the AI did
   :   It wrote a first job advert for a warehouse worker.

       Why: It says what the AI made.

   What you changed
   :   I wrote two tasks in my own words.

       Why: It says what is yours.

   How you checked
   :   I checked that every requirement is about the job.

       Why: It says how you checked the AI's work.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/prompt-cleaner.html" poster="sims/prompt-cleaner.png" title="Prompt Cleaner: no personal data in the chat" >}}

3. In **Prompt Cleaner**, clean **Huda's reminder**. Which parts get a
   placeholder, and which stay?

   {{< record "Placeholders: … ; what stays: …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   The name becomes **[Customer]**, the e-mail **[e-mail]** and the bank
   account **[bank account]**. **340 JD** and **March** stay: the AI needs
   them, and they say nothing about who the person is.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   A placeholder, or keep it? Sort the parts of Huda's reminder.

   Replace with a placeholder
   :   the name of the customer

       Why: A name shows who the person is.

   :   the bank account

       Why: Bank details are private.

   Keep: the AI needs it
   :   340 JD

       Why: The amount says nothing about who the person is.

   :   March

       Why: The month is needed for the reminder.
   :::
